extracted.intended_audience: analysts and decisionmakers in U.S. Federal regulatory agencies (agency rulewriters and regulatory analysts)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing regulatory analyses (RIAs) to evaluate benefits, costs, alternatives, and uncertainties for Federal rulemakings, including required specialized analyses under statutes and Executive Orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key elements of a regulatory analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A good regulatory analysis should include the following three basic elements: (1) a statement of the need for the proposed action, (2) an examination of alternative approaches, and (3) an evaluation of the benefits and costs—quantitative and qualitative—of the proposed action and the main alternatives identified by the analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complete analysis includes discussion of non-quantified as well as quantified benefits and costs, links between actions and expected benefits, a clearly stated baseline, identification of ancillary effects, and a summary of benefit and cost estimates for each alternative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of need and demonstration of necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Before recommending Federal regulatory action, an agency must demonstrate that the proposed action is necessary and identify the problem the action intends to address (including market failures or other social purposes) and assess the significance of that problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the intervention results from statutory or judicial directive, describe authority, extent of discretion, and regulatory instruments; explain whether addressing a market failure or other compelling public need; quantify where feasible and demonstrate likelihood of net good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and justify baseline(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify a baseline. Benefits and costs are defined in comparison with a clearly stated alternative. This normally will be a 'no action' baseline; comparisons to a 'next best' alternative are also useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State what the world will be like if the proposed rule is not adopted; use baselines consistently across alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link regulatory actions to expected benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain how the actions required by the rule are linked to the expected benefits (e.g., indicate how additional safety equipment will reduce safety risks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform similar linkage analyses for each alternative; document causal chains and mechanisms by which regulation yields benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify ancillary benefits and undesirable side‑effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the expected undesirable side-effects and ancillary benefits of the proposed regulatory action and the alternatives; add these to direct benefits and costs as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider indirect, spillover, and distributional effects and include them in monetized, quantified-but-not-monetized, or qualitative categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of non‑quantified effects and threshold (break‑even) analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: When not all important benefits and costs can be expressed in monetary units, indicate which non-quantified effects are most important and, where appropriate, carry out a 'threshold' or 'break-even' analysis to evaluate their significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how small or large non-quantified values would have to be to change the net-benefit conclusion; recommend which non-quantified factors merit consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder consultation and early outreach
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek out the opinions of those who will be affected by the regulation and individuals/organizations with special knowledge or insight; consultation should occur early and not be limited to final stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use consultation to identify relevant issues, obtain data, and improve quality of analysis; document consultations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of assumptions, methods, and inputs
rubrics_metrics.description: A good analysis is transparent: state assumptions (time horizon, discount rates), present sensitivity analyses, and make it possible for a qualified third party to see how estimates and conclusions were derived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit assumptions, data sources, model documentation, and appendices; include executive summary and standardized accounting statement; disclose limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide full documentation and references
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide specific references to all sources of data, appendices with documentation of models (where necessary), and results of formal sensitivity and other uncertainty analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include source citations (RIA, preamble, etc.), and make detailed documentation available on request or as appendices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate why federal action is preferable to alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider alternatives to Federal regulation (antitrust, litigation, administrative compensation) and whether State or local regulation is more appropriate; show that Federal regulation is the best way to solve the problem when claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the appropriateness of the level of government, potential gains from diversity vs costs of fragmentation, and impacts on international harmonization and trade barriers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and analyze market failures and other social purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: If regulation is intended to correct market failures, describe the failure qualitatively and (where feasible) quantitatively; consider externalities, common property resources/public goods, market power, and inadequate/asymmetric information; also describe other social purposes (efficiency of government, redistribution, anti-discrimination, privacy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document evidence for the existence of a failure (not merely its theoretical possibility); explain strengths and limitations of intangible rationales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption against certain types of economic regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: A particularly demanding burden of proof is required to demonstrate the need for price controls in competitive markets; production or sales quotas in competitive markets; mandatory uniform quality standards if voluntary/disclosure measures would suffice; or controls on entry into employment or production (except narrowly justified cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid regulations that increase market power unless justified; provide strong evidence when proposing these forms of economic regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider statutory range of alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: When a statute establishes a specific regulatory requirement and the agency is considering a more stringent standard, examine benefits and costs of reasonable alternatives reflecting the agency's statutory discretion, including the specific statutory requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the statutory minimum (or specified standard) as an alternative for comparison in the RIA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider different compliance dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine how timing and compliance dates affect net benefits; different implementation dates can change benefits (e.g., preventing stock declines) and costs (lead times for industries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model several compliance-date scenarios to capture timing tradeoffs and identify lower-cost ways to achieve objectives (e.g., sufficient lead time).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider different enforcement and monitoring methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate alternative enforcement frameworks (on-site inspections, periodic reporting, penalties, random or parametric monitoring) and choose the most cost-effective enforcement approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze costs and effectiveness of monitoring options and consider appropriate incentives for compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate different degrees of stringency
rubrics_metrics.description: Study alternative levels of regulatory stringency to understand relationships between stringency and the size and distribution of benefits and costs across groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure marginal costs and marginal benefits across stringency levels to find efficient points; consider distributional implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different requirements by firm size
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider setting different requirements for large and small firms based on estimated differences in compliance costs or expected benefits; rules with significant impacts on many small entities trigger Regulatory Flexibility Act requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inefficiently loading costs onto most productive firms; consult RFA guidance and SBA Chief Counsel for Advocacy as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different requirements by geographic region
rubrics_metrics.description: Where benefits and costs vary significantly across regions, consider different regional requirements rather than uniform national standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh gains from tailoring rules regionally against costs of regulatory fragmentation and increased compliance costs for multi-state firms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer performance standards over design standards where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Performance standards express outcomes rather than means and generally give regulated parties flexibility to meet objectives cost-effectively; account for monitoring/compliance costs as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess cost savings of flexibility against enforcement/monitoring costs and potential local adverse outcomes ('hot spots').

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider market‑oriented approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Explore economic-incentive approaches such as fees, penalties, subsidies, marketable permits/offsets, changes in liability or property rights, bonds/insurance/warranties, and averaging/banking/trading (ABT) programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate potential cost reductions and distributional effects; ensure ABT or trading does not produce unacceptable local outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider informational measures before prescriptive regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: If market failure arises from inadequate/asymmetric information, prefer informational remedies (standardized testing/rating systems, mandatory or voluntary disclosure, government provision of information) where effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate benefits and costs of informational measures, including costs of gathering/communicating information and potential displacement or misinterpretation of information; when uncertain, use the least intrusive sufficient informational alternative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate analytical approach: BCA and CEA
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Benefit-Cost Analysis (BCA) and Cost-Effectiveness Analysis (CEA) as systematic frameworks; major health/safety rulemakings should have CEA (when valid effectiveness measures exist) and BCA where monetary values can be assigned; for other major rulemakings, carry out BCA and CEA if primary benefits cannot be monetized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where no quantified information is possible, present qualitative discussion; strive for analytical consistency across regulations and agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: BCA fundamentals and incremental analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: In BCA both benefits and costs are expressed in monetary units; measure incremental benefits and costs of successively more stringent alternatives to identify the alternative that maximizes net benefits; avoid relying on benefit-cost ratios as indicators of net benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When benefits/costs cannot be monetized, measure in physical units or describe qualitatively; use professional judgment for non-quantified factors and consider threshold analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: CEA fundamentals and incremental cost‑effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: CEA compares options with the same primary outcome using cost per unit of effectiveness; use incremental (not average) cost-effectiveness to compare mutually exclusive alternatives and avoid mistakes from average ratios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include all relevant societal costs (public and private), subtract monetized ancillary benefits from gross costs to compute net costs, avoid double-counting, and choose final outcome measures when possible (lives saved, life-years) rather than intermediate outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing effectiveness metrics for health and safety
rubrics_metrics.description: When CEA is applied to public health and safety rulemakings, select measures (e.g., lives saved, life-years saved, QALYs, equivalent lives) that capture mortality and morbidity; consider fairness and appropriate adjustments so metrics do not unfairly undervalue groups (e.g., disabled populations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB does not require a specific measure; report multiple measures when useful and explain selection. Prefer population averages for adjustments rather than subgroup-dominated values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of benefits and costs over time (discounting, reporting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Present undiscounted streams of annual benefit and cost estimates for each year of the analytic horizon and present annualized benefits and costs using real discount rates of 3% and 7%; report all monetized effects in 2001 dollars and convert other-year dollars using the GDP deflator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stream should begin in the year the final rule will begin to have effects; report both undiscounted and discounted annualized figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of risk and uncertainty; sensitivity analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide expected-value estimates and distributions where possible, and perform sensitivity analyses to reveal robustness and 'switch points' at which conclusions change; change one variable at a time or vary combinations to test robustness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If nontrivial uncertainty exists, present alternative plausible assumptions and explain critical dependencies; add footnotes or appendices as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal probabilistic analysis for complex or very large rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply formal probabilistic analysis (e.g., Monte Carlo simulation, expert elicitation/Delphi) where there are large/multiple uncertainties or cascading effects; required for rules exceeding the $1 billion annual threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify probability distributions of key parameters, account for correlated inputs (do not assume independence by default), and portray probabilistic results clearly in graphs/tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic valuation of uncertain outcomes and risk preference
rubrics_metrics.description: When outcomes have distributions, combine probability distributions to provide estimated benefits and costs; emphasize summary statistics readily understood (expected values) while acknowledging assumptions about societal risk neutrality or explaining departures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume risk neutrality generally; if adopting different risk-preference assumptions, justify them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision and rounding of estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported estimates should reflect the precision of the analysis; rounding should be consistent with implied precision (examples: $220 million rounded to nearest $10 million; $222 million to nearest $1 million).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communicate implied precision (e.g., +/-) and avoid false precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate reporting of transfers versus welfare effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Report transfers separately and avoid misclassifying transfer payments as benefits or costs; identify transfers 'on-budget' (from whom to whom) and 'off-budget' and use categories to describe redistributive effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If transfers have efficiency effects in addition to distributional effects, report them accordingly; distinguish Federal budget transfers from private-party transfers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report distributional impacts (state/local/tribal, small business, wages, growth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify portions of benefits, costs, and transfers received by State, local, and tribal governments; to the extent feasible, identify effects on small businesses, wages, and economic growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules with annual costs under $1 billion likely have minimal growth effects, but report these effects where feasible; note Regulatory Flexibility Act triggers for small entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting statement and standardized reporting format
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide an accounting statement with tables reporting benefit and cost estimates for each major final rule (categories: monetized benefits; annualized quantified but not monetized; qualitative unquantified benefits; analogous cost categories; transfers; effects by recipient).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow suggested formats, report primary/minimum/maximum estimates, provide source citations (RIA, preamble), and include separate rows for state/local/tribal effects and small-business impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized statutory and executive‑order analyses (RFA, Unfunded Mandates, Paperwork)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of and perform specialized analyses required by law and Executive Orders, including Regulatory Flexibility Act analyses for significant impacts on small entities, Unfunded Mandates Act statements for >$100 million impacts on governments/private sector, and Paperwork Reduction Act assessments for information collections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate with agency counsel and SBA Advocacy Office; consult agency CIO for Paperwork Reduction Act compliance and seek OMB approvals where required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information quality and data standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Data and analysis used to support rules must meet agency and OMB government-wide information quality guidelines; agencies should ensure information quality performance goals are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult agency guidelines, OMB's Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs, and agency CIO/Statistical and Science Policy Branch as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental review and NEPA compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider environmental impacts under NEPA; prepare environmental impact statements for major Federal actions significantly affecting the quality of the human environment and complete NEPA documentation before issuing a final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow CEQ regulations (40 C.F.R. 1500-1508) and associated guidance, and coordinate NEPA documentation with rulemaking schedule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider impacts on children (Executive Order 13045)
rubrics_metrics.description: For economically significant rules concerning environmental health or safety risks that may disproportionately affect children, provide OMB/OIRA an evaluation of the effects on children and an explanation why the planned regulation is preferable to other feasible alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address disproportionate risks to children to the extent permitted by law and consistent with agency mission; document analyses presented to OIRA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider energy impacts (Executive Order 13211)
rubrics_metrics.description: For significant energy actions, prepare and submit to OMB a Statement of Energy Effects including detailed statements of any adverse effects on energy supply, distribution, or use and publish the statement or a summary in the NPRM and final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow OMB Memorandum guidance on implementing EO 13211 and coordinate reporting/publication requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unfunded Mandates Act threshold and analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare a written statement about benefits and costs prior to issuing a proposed or final rule that may result in aggregate expenditures by state/local/tribal governments or the private sector of $100,000,000 or more in any one year (adjusted for inflation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytical requirements under Executive Order 12866 are similar; reuse analyses where possible to comply with both requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: RFA and small-entity analyses and consultation (SBREFA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Regulatory Flexibility Act, prepare proposed and final 'regulatory flexibility analysis' if the rule could have a significant impact on a substantial number of small entities; notify SBA Chief Counsel for Advocacy of draft rules with significant impacts; EPA/OSHA must consult small business under SBREFA before proposing certain rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post RFAs on the internet for public review and give appropriate consideration to Advocacy Office comments; consult agency guidance on preparing RFAs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision in monetary reporting and unit conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Report monetized effects in a common price year (2001 dollars in this Circular) and convert other years using GDP deflator; present both undiscounted annual streams and annualized discounted figures at 3% and 7% real discount rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify the analytic time horizon, year effects begin, and present alternative discounting results to illustrate sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of alternative mortality valuation estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: When estimating the value of reductions in premature mortality risk, present alternative primary estimates (different VSL or valuation approaches) to reflect uncertainty and to show sensitivity of results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report alternative primary estimates and explain the rationale for the values used; include sensitivity or scenario results using alternative valuations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid double‑counting and clearly define cost concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the numerator in cost-effectiveness ratios and cost estimates reflects net costs (gross compliance costs minus any cost savings) and avoid double-counting effects in both numerator and denominator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reduce gross costs by monetized values already used in effectiveness denominators (e.g., life-years).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting probabilistic and distributional results clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Portray probabilistic results—in graphs and/or tables—clearly and meaningfully so users can understand distributions, confidence bounds, and implications for decisionmaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When providing only upper/lower bounds, use 95% and 5% confidence bounds where possible; make detailed distributions available on request.
